source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) Generative Language Modeling for Automated Theorem Proving (GPT-f)
finding: GPT-f, a transformer prover run inside a kernel-checked Metamath search, beat the prior learned prover on held-out theorems. Every proof is checked by the Metamath verifier.
numbers: 56.22% of held-out set.mm test theorems vs 21.16% for MetaGen-IL. Search width a=2,4,8,16,32: 42.90, 47.29, 51.26, 54.05, 56.50 (gains +4.39, +3.97, +2.99, +2.45 per doubling).
limits: Metamath has simple string-substitution rules; may not carry to Lean or Isabelle. Random split: test theorems can appear as lemmas of training theorems.
agent_relevance: Kernel verdicts give a clean pass/fail signal for S8. More search width kept helping but with falling returns.

source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) GPT-f, pretraining ablation
finding: Pretraining on math text and code helped. Right-kind data beat raw scale.
numbers: 160m from scratch 28.96%; 160m +WebMath 34.79%; 700m from scratch 31.58%; 700m +WebMath 42.56%; 1.5B +WebMath 42.39% (no gain over 700m).
limits: One run per cell, no variance reported. Gain from scale stalled between 700m and 1.5B.
agent_relevance: Domain-matched context matters more than size. Relevant to what we put in the prompt for a proof-checking step.

source: Polu & Sutskever (2020) GPT-f, synthetic data
finding: Adding the model's own verified proofs to training hurt when it was too much.
numbers: Synthetic proofs were about 1% of training data; raising them to 5% hurt performance at the model sizes studied.
limits: Small models, early method.
agent_relevance: Do not flood context with the agent's own past verified output; keep it a small share.

source: Han et al. (2022) PACT: Proof Artifact Co-Training
finding: Training on auxiliary tasks taken from Lean proof terms raised held-out proof success in Lean 3. A control showed it was not mere regularization.
numbers: Success on mathlib test theorems 32% to 48.4% (837m, WebMath>mix1+mix2+tactic). WebMath>tactic with 15% residual dropout: 33.6%. Model sizes: 121m 35.1%, 163m 39.8%, 837m 48.4%.
limits: Overfitting on the tactic data set in within about one epoch. Random split inflates; see next line.
agent_relevance: Auxiliary data was worth about +16 points; a bigger model about +4 to +8.

source: Han et al. (2022) PACT, temporal hold-out and contamination audit
finding: On theorems added after the pretraining data was gathered, success dropped somewhat. A temporally held-out set (future-mathlib) showed many easy boilerplate lemmas.
numbers: Post-18 Apr 2020 theorems (1,350): 45.6%. Post-11 Sep 2020 (544): 43.3%. Overall 48.4%. future-mathlib: refl alone 11.6% (328), tidy-bfs 21.8% (611), best model 37.1% (1043), and it proved 94% of the refl lemmas.
limits: The authors say leakage explains little. Test theorems in a random split can serve as lemmas in training proofs.
agent_relevance: Report on post-cutoff items. Pass rates fall a few points once leakage is controlled.

source: Zheng, Han & Polu (2022) miniF2F: cross-system benchmark
finding: 488 olympiad-level statements (244 valid, 244 test) formalized in several proof systems. Same problems are far easier in Lean than Metamath for the same model class.
numbers: GPT-f Lean test: pass@1 24.6%, pass@8 29.2% (valid 23.9% / 29.3%). Lean tidy baseline test 1.3% pass@1. GPT-f Metamath test: 1.3% pass@1, 1.6% pass@8. Prior mathlib split 10.5%.
limits: Statement formalization errors existed; later repos fix them.
agent_relevance: The proof language is part of the capability. Choose the formal target language with care.

source: Jiang et al. (2022) Thor: Wielding Hammers to Integrate Language Models and Automated Theorem Provers
finding: Letting a language model call Sledgehammer as a step beat either alone on Isabelle PISA.
numbers: LM alone 39.0%, Sledgehammer alone 25.7%, union 48.8%, Thor 57.0%; 8.2% of problems solved only by Thor. LISA 33.2%. Ablations 55.4%, 53.6%, T=1.0 sampling 55.7%. miniF2F test: LM 24.2%, Thor 29.9% (+5.7) vs expert-iterated PACT 29.6% (+5.0).
limits: Only 1.9% of LM steps that name premises advanced the proof vs 28.2% of steps with no premises. PISA is one library (AFP, 4% test split).
agent_relevance: A cheap checked tool call beats model guessing. Facts the model names itself are unreliable, so route them to a tool (G2).

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Draft, Sketch, and Prove (DSP)
finding: Informal proof draft, formal sketch with holes, then an automated prover closes the holes. Large gain over Sledgehammer alone. Ablations show what matters.
numbers: miniF2F valid/test: Sledgehammer 9.9/10.4, with heuristics 18.0/20.9; DSP with human informal proof 42.6/39.3 (200 of 488 solved); Codex informal 40.6/35.3. Ablation drops valid/test: no in-line comments -4.9/-2.8; no informal proofs -3.7/-5.3; no automated prover -9.8/-9.0. No sketching solves 154.
limits: Isabelle only. Sample budgets differ from rivals.
agent_relevance: The prover closing leaf goals matters most; informal plan adds about 4-5 points. Plan at the top, verify at the leaves.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) DSP, model-written informal proofs and saturation
finding: Model-written informal proofs were about as good as human ones, and a bigger writer did not help on test.
numbers: Minerva 8B 40.6/36.5, 62B 43.9/37.7, 540B 42.6/38.9 (valid/test); 199 solved by 62B and 540B vs 200 for human. Success plateaus after about 70 autoformalization attempts (about 50 without comments, solving 181).
limits: Test-set rates fell as the writer grew from 62B to 540B in one pair; no variance reported.
agent_relevance: Attempts saturate; a counted stop rule beats sampling forever.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HyperTree Proof Search for Neural Theorem Proving
finding: Online training from the model's own proof searches plus hypertree search raised Metamath and Lean rates.
numbers: Metamath: supervised valid 65.4% / test 61.2% vs GPT-f 56.5 / 56.2; online training raises valid cumulative to 82.6%; test pass@32 55.8% to 65.6%. Lean: miniF2F-valid 58.6% cumulative (statements seen in training); test pass@64 41.0% vs GPT-f 36.6%; without synthetic co-training 54.9% and 38.5%. After 7 days 139 of 327 curriculum statements (GPT-f 100). Equations: 91.3% vs a supervised model never above 36%.
limits: Valid numbers are cumulative over training, not held out. About 1360 A100 days of training.
agent_relevance: The held-out gain is the test row (+4.4 on Lean). Cumulative on seen items inflates. Needs weight updates, so the scaffold cannot copy it.

source: Lample et al. (2022) HTPS, online versus fixed model
finding: A fixed model given the same number of attempts plateaus; a model updated between attempts keeps improving.
numbers: Metamath valid: supervised plateau 66%, online training above 74% after 7 days. Reloading more often converged faster and higher.
limits: Needs training.
agent_relevance: Repeated identical attempts plateau. In prompt-only form, change the context (add the checker message), not just the seed.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo: Theorem Proving with Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
finding: Premise retrieval helps. Random splits are inflated by near-duplicate theorems; a novel_premises split halves the score.
numbers: Pass@1 random / novel_premises: tidy 23.8/5.3; GPT-4 zero-shot 29.0/7.4; ReProver 51.2/26.3; ReProver without retrieval 47.6/23.2. miniF2F test 26.5% (PACT 25.9%); ProofNet 13.8% (48/349).
limits: GPT-4 may have seen mathlib proofs. Single run pass@1.
agent_relevance: Use hold-outs that block memorized duplicates. Retrieval adds +3.6 and +3.1 points.

source: Yang et al. (2023) LeanDojo, tooling error rate
finding: The earlier Lean environment lean-gym wrongly judged many correct proofs as wrong.
numbers: lean-gym misjudged 21.1% of correct human proofs; LeanDojo 1.4%.
limits: Applies to the old tool at the time.
agent_relevance: Verify the verifier. A bad harness can reject one in five correct answers and distort every reported rate.

source: First et al. (2023) Baldur: Whole-Proof Generation and Repair with Large Language Models
finding: Whole-proof generation by a fine-tuned LLM matches search provers and complements them. Feeding the checker error back for repair gives a small gain.
numbers: Isabelle PISA: 8b generate 34.8% at 16 samples, 40.7% at 64; with theory-file context 47.5%; 62b with context 47.9% (+0.4); Baldur union Thor 65.7% (Thor alone 58.0%). Repair with the checker error: generate+repair 24.9%, second repair 26.2% (+1.3), vs plain generation 25.4% at equal cost 3 (+0.8). By area with context: mathematics 41.9->50.5, logic 51.6->53.6, tools 53.9->51.8.
limits: Repair training data did not mirror the edits needed. Coq Diva reached 33.8% on its own benchmark; rates are not comparable across systems.
agent_relevance: Real checker error plus one repair: small but real gain (+0.8 to +1.5). Context (+6.8) matters more than model size (+0.4).

source: Azerbayev et al. (2023) ProofNet: Autoformalizing and Formally Proving Undergraduate-Level Mathematics
finding: Statement formalization is itself hard for models.
numbers: Codex few-shot correctly formalized 13.4% of theorem statements; proofGPT-1.3B formalized none correctly.
limits: Scoring of formalizations done by hand on a small set.
agent_relevance: A kernel-checked proof of a wrong statement is still a pass. G3 means check the statement too.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover: Advancing Theorem Proving in LLMs through Large-Scale Synthetic Data
finding: Large synthetic autoformalized data plus iterative expert training lifted whole-proof generation in Lean 4. A fifth of the machine-written statements were wrong.
numbers: miniF2F-test: 46.3% at 64 samples; greedy 30.03% rising to 50.0% at 65,536 samples; cumulative 52.0% (valid 60.2%). GPT-4 23.0% at 64; HTPS 41.0%. FIMO 5 of 148.
limits: At least 20% of generated formal statements were incorrect even after filtering. Table columns were garbled in text extraction.
agent_relevance: A verifier cannot rescue an unprovable goal. Detect futile goals early (impasse signal).

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5: Harnessing Proof Assistant Feedback for RL and MCTS
finding: Truncate at the first Lean error, resume from the last valid tactic; RMaxTS tree search; RL on proof-assistant feedback.
numbers: miniF2F-test: V1 50.0% to V1.5-RL 60.2% single pass; 51.6% at 128 samples; RMaxTS 62.7% (SFT with CoT and RMaxTS about 59.0%, +3.7 for RL). ProofNet test 22.6% to 25.3% (valid 21.6 to 25.4); ReProver 13.8%, InternLM2-StepProver 18.1%.
limits: Budgets of thousands of samples. Authors say RL here is a genuine capability gain, unlike RL for natural-language math.
agent_relevance: The checker is used to locate the first error (G2). Tree search adds a modest +2.5 on a strong model.

source: Xin et al. (2024) DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5, chain-of-thought mode
finding: Short natural-language reasoning before each proof step beat no reasoning, and the advantage grew with the sample budget. The two modes are complementary.
numbers: RL averaged 51.6% on miniF2F and 18.2% on ProofNet at pass@128; CoT above non-CoT in most settings; mixing both modes scored highest (up to 62.7% with RMaxTS).
limits: Exact per-budget table garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: A plan before code diversifies attempts; the verifier still decides.

source: Kimina-Prover team (2025) Kimina-Prover Preview
finding: RL on a think-then-write-Lean format gave large miniF2F gains and strong sample efficiency.
numbers: miniF2F-test 72B: pass@1 52.94%, pass@8 68.85%, pass@32 77.87% (from table), pass@1024 80.74% vs BFS-Prover 72.95%, Goedel-Prover-SFT 64.7% (25,600 samples), DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5-RL 60.2%. 72B over 7B: +0.44, +5.75, +7.87 at three budgets.
limits: Table rows interleave in extraction so pass@k labels may shift by one; format rule asks Lean code to cover at least 60% of the reasoning.
agent_relevance: Reasoning trace before code is part of the best recipe; more samples help with diminishing returns.

source: Seed-Prover team (2025) Seed-Prover: Deep and Broad Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
finding: Lemma-style proving with Lean compiler feedback, a pool of proved lemmas and self-summarization saturates miniF2F and jumps on PutnamBench.
numbers: MiniF2F-valid 100.0%, test 99.6% (medium) vs 90.6% / 92.2% prior; PutnamBench 331/657 medium, 201/657 light vs 86/657 prior; past IMO 78.1% (47/55 easy, 47/56 medium, 27/44 hard; algebra 72/85, number theory 42/55, combinatorics 7/14); CombiBench 30.0% vs 10.0%; MiniCTX-v2 81.8% vs 44.3% (o4-mini).
limits: Heavy test-time compute. Combinatorics weakest. Developer-reported, not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: A pool of already verified lemmas is code-held state for S8; effort scales with a counted budget level.

source: Tsoukalas et al. (2024) PutnamBench: Evaluating Neural Theorem-Provers on the Putnam Mathematical Competition
finding: Harder benchmark (Putnam) in Lean 4, Isabelle and Coq: 2024 methods solved only a handful.
numbers: Lean 640 problems: GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, ReProver 0 with or without retrieval. Isabelle: GPT-4 1, DSP 4, Sledgehammer 3. Coq 412 problems: GPT-4 1, COPRA 1, Tactician 0, CoqHammer 0. Only Putnam 1988 B1 solved in both Lean and Coq.
limits: Benchmark of 2024. Seed-Prover later reported 331/657, about 4x the best prior (86) and about 50x these 2024 counts.
agent_relevance: Ceilings move within a year; do not treat one year's number as a stable limit.

source: Ringer et al. (2020) QED at Large: A Survey of Engineering of Formally Verified Software
finding: Verified software can be more reliable than tested software but costs large human proof effort; the trusted base still includes specifications and the checker.
numbers: seL4 initial correctness proofs about 20 person-years; 480,000 lines of specification and proof scripts by 2014. Csmith found 79 bugs in GCC and 202 in LLVM and none in verified parts of CompCert.
limits: Only verified parts of CompCert. Pollack's question of whether a formal statement has its intended meaning remains.
agent_relevance: The kernel guarantees derivability, not meaning. Keep a statement check in the scaffold.

source: Staples et al. (2014) Productivity for proof engineering
finding: Across nine L4.verified projects, proof effort in person-weeks rises linearly with lines of proof script, across projects and individuals.
numbers: Nine projects; strong linear relation (no coefficient on the abstract page).
limits: Lines of proof are an imperfect size measure; the abstract page gives no correlation value; only the abstract page was read.
agent_relevance: Human proof cost scales with proof size; budget agent effort in proportion.

source: Matichuk et al. (2015) Empirical study towards a leading indicator for cost of formal software verification
finding: Proof size grows quadratically with the size of the formal statement.
numbers: 15,018 lemmas, about 215,000 lines of proof script, from seL4 and the two largest software-verification entries in the Archive of Formal Proofs.
limits: No R-squared on the abstract page; Isabelle only; only the abstract page was read.
agent_relevance: Long goals cost super-linearly. Split goals before attempting them.

source: Yang & Deng (2019) Learning to Prove Theorems via Interacting with Proof Assistants (CoqGym, ASTactic)
finding: Learned tactic prover for Coq on human proofs from many projects. The hammer and the learned model complement each other.
numbers: ASTactic proves 12.2% of test theorems; CoqHammer 24.8% with extended time; combined 30.0% (+5.2 over hammer); a baseline under 4.9%.
limits: Split is by project, harder than theorem-wise splits in other papers.
agent_relevance: Combine the symbolic tool with the learned model. Project-wise splits give lower, more honest rates.

source: Bohme & Nipkow (2010) Sledgehammer: Judgement Day (search-result summary only)
finding: Evaluation of Isabelle's Sledgehammer with E, SPASS and Vampire on goals from 7 Isabelle theories.
numbers: About 1200 goals (a secondary source says 1240); 48% reconstructed proofs with three first-order provers, 2 minutes each; Blanchet later note: 38% on goals not provable by standard automation.
limits: Page fetch failed; numbers come from a search snippet and need checking in LNCS 6173 pp. 107-121.
agent_relevance: Hammers are a strong cheap baseline that LLM provers add to (see Thor).
